question.explanation: Lung sounds (diminished bilaterally with crackles in the bases), the elevated temperature, and the complaint of chest pain with coughing are all indicative of respiratory alterations consistent with tuberculosis.

question.stem: For each assessment finding, click to specify if the finding is a risk factor or is not a risk factor for tuberculosis infection.
question.footnote: Taken from the Maryland Next Gen NCLEX Test Bank Project, University of Maryland School of Nursing: “Tuberculosis” medical-surgical faculty case study (Elizabeth Mackessy-Lloyd, DNP, RN, CNE, Hood University, September 1, 2022). question.explanation:
Asia is a high-risk area for tuberculosis, and living in close quarters with others (extended travel with a tour group) is a risk factor, as are the elevated temperature, cough, and complaints of chest pain.
Being overweight, the home medication list, and the blood pressure are not risk factors for tuberculosis infection.

question.preamble: The client is diagnosed with a tuberculosis infection, and orders for new medications are received. The nurse has reviewed the Orders.
question.explanation:
An N95 respirator protects the nurse from airborne transmission of tuberculosis. Coughing and deep breathing is an important nursing intervention for this client, and the client should be encouraged to wear a face mask around others for at least the first 3 weeks of treatment.
While contact tracing would be done for close contacts, the nurse would not reveal the client's identity. The other interventions are not appropriate for this client.

leftContent.intro: A 48-year-old female client presents to the outpatient clinic in response to contact tracing for possible tuberculosis exposure.

question.stem: For each client teaching point, click to specify whether the information needs to be provided immediately, at the time of client follow-up, or is not indicated for this client.

rows.text: “Your cholesterol is high, and we need to discuss your diet.”
“You will need to take the medications every day for at least 4 months.”
“If you continue to cough at home, please save all of your sputum.”
“You will need to have regular labs to check the effects of this medication on your liver.”
“Try to pace your activities to preserve your energy.”
“Tuberculosis is not spread by germs on dishes or linens.”
“Your A1C is high, and you may have diabetes.”

question.footnote: Taken from the Maryland Next Gen NCLEX Test Bank Project, University of Maryland School of Nursing: “Tuberculosis” medical-surgical faculty case study (Elizabeth Mackessy-Lloyd, DNP, RN, CNE, Hood University, September 1, 2022). Available at https://www.nursing.umaryland.edu/mnwc/initiatives/nextgen-nclex/nextgen-nclex-library/ (Faculty Case Studies). Laboratory values shown in SI units.
question.explanation:
Teaching about the medication schedule and length of treatment, liver monitoring, energy conservation, and how tuberculosis is (and is not) spread is needed immediately.
The cholesterol is high and the A1C is elevated but in the prediabetes range. These should be addressed at the follow-up visit, when the client may be more able to receive information unrelated to the presenting problem.
There is no need to collect sputum at home since the antibiotics have already been started.

tabs.title: Progress Notes
tabs.content: Client returns for a follow-up appointment 4 weeks after being diagnosed with a tuberculosis infection. Reports missing several doses of medication. Continues to have a productive cough and is tired most days. Lung sounds clear with few scattered crackles. Rates pain with the cough at 3/10. VS: T 98.8° F (37.1° C), P 80 beats/min, RR 22 breaths/min, BP 144/88 mm Hg, pulse oximetry reading 95% on room air. Repeat WBC 9.0 × 109/L. Chest X-ray shows mild pleural effusion in the right base.
